s2-micro-01.stem: The graph shows the market for home-health aides, where a single hospital system is the only employer in the region. To maximize profit, how many aides should the hospital system hire, and what hourly wage will it pay?
s2-micro-01.stimulus: {"kind":"graph","description":"Labor market for home-health aides with one hospital system as the only employer. Upward-sloping labor supply, steeper marginal factor cost, and downward-sloping marginal revenue product curves.","data":{"x_axis":{"label":"Number of aides hired (L)","range":[0,40],"unit":"aides"},"y_axis":{"label":"Hourly wage / value ($ per hour)","range":[0,40],"unit":"dollars per hour"},"curves":[{"label":"Labor supply (S)","equation":"W = 8 + 0.5L","points":[[0,8],[16,16],[24,20],[40,28]]},{"label":"Marginal factor cost (MFC)","equation":"MFC = 8 + L","points":[[0,8],[16,24],[24,32]]},{"label":"Marginal revenue product (MRP)","equation":"MRP = 32 - 0.5L","points":[[0,32],[16,24],[24,20],[40,12]]}],"notes":"The hospital system is the only employer of aides in the region and must pay all aides the same wage."}

options.text: 16 aides at $20 per hour
options.why: Uses the correct quantity but pays the competitive wage; the misconception is that a monopsonist still pays the wage where supply meets MRP.

options.text: 16 aides at $24 per hour
options.why: Reads the wage from the MRP/MFC intersection ($24) instead of dropping down to the supply curve; the misconception is that the monopsonist pays workers their marginal revenue product.

options.text: 16 aides at $16 per hour
options.why: Correct: hire where MRP = MFC (16 aides, both $24), then read the wage from the supply curve at 16 aides ($16).

options.text: 24 aides at $20 per hour
options.why: Gives the competitive outcome where supply equals MRP; the misconception is that monopsony does not change employment or wage.

options.text: 24 aides at $16 per hour
options.why: Combines the competitive quantity with the monopsony wage; the misconception is mixing the MRP = supply rule for quantity with the supply-curve wage reading.

s2-micro-01.explanation_en: A profit-maximizing monopsonist hires up to the point where marginal revenue product equals marginal factor cost: 32 - 0.5L = 8 + L gives L = 16, where both equal $24. The wage is the lowest the workers will accept for 16 aides, read from the supply curve: 8 + 0.5(16) = $16. Paying $24 per hour confuses the MFC/MRP value with the wage, since the monopsonist does not need to pay that much. Paying $20 uses the competitive wage, which the monopsonist is not forced to pay. Hiring 24 aides at $20 is the competitive outcome, which would arise only if the hospital could not set the wage by restricting hiring. Hiring 24 aides at $16 mixes the competitive quantity with the monopsony wage, but at 24 aides the supply curve gives $20, not $16, and MFC ($32) exceeds MRP ($20).

s2-micro-02.stem: Based on the table, at the profit-maximizing output the seller earns a positive economic profit. Given free entry into this market, which of the following best explains what will happen over time?
s2-micro-02.stimulus: {"kind":"table","description":"Short-run data for a honey seller at a farmers' market, a monopolistically competitive firm. Marginal cost is constant at $8 per jar.","data":{"columns":["Quantity (jars per day)","Price ($)","Marginal revenue ($)","Marginal cost ($)","Average total cost ($)"],"rows":[[8,16,12,8,13.5],[10,15,10,8,12],[12,14,8,8,11],[14,13,6,8,10.5],[16,12,4,8,10.25]],"note":"Demand curve is P = 20 - 0.5Q, so MR = 20 - Q. Market has free entry by sellers of similar but differentiated honey."}

options.text: Entry increases total market demand, shifting this firm's demand curve right, so its economic profit grows larger over time.
options.why: Misconception: confuses entry with market growth; entry takes customers from existing firms and does not raise their demand.

options.text: Entry of close substitutes shifts this firm's demand left and makes it more elastic until price equals average total cost and economic profit is zero.
options.why: Correct: positive profit attracts entrants with close substitutes, so each firm's demand falls and becomes more elastic until P = ATC, giving zero economic profit.

options.text: Existing firms exit because of the positive profit, which shifts this firm's demand left until its marginal revenue equals its marginal cost.
options.why: Misconception: reverses the entry/exit signal; positive profit attracts entry, not exit.

options.text: Entry leaves this firm's demand unchanged, but its marginal cost rises with the added competition until economic profit falls to zero.
options.why: Misconception: believes competition changes costs rather than demand; the adjustment works through the demand curve.

options.text: Entry shifts this firm's demand left until price equals marginal cost, so the firm ends up producing at the efficient scale.
options.why: Misconception: applies the perfect competition result; in monopolistic competition P stays above MC in the long run, with excess capacity.

s2-micro-02.explanation_en: MR = MC at Q = 12, where P = $14 and ATC = $11, so profit is (14 - 11) x 12 = $36 per day. Positive economic profit attracts new sellers of close substitutes. Each firm loses customers, so its demand shifts left and becomes more elastic. Entry continues until the demand curve is tangent to ATC, where P = ATC and economic profit is zero. The option saying demand shifts right is wrong because entry takes sales from existing firms. The option saying firms exit is wrong because positive profit induces entry. The option saying marginal cost rises is wrong because the adjustment comes through demand. The option saying price equals marginal cost is wrong because the long-run tangency occurs where price exceeds marginal cost, leaving excess capacity.

s2-micro-03.stem: Based on the graph, which of the following correctly describes the unregulated market outcome relative to the socially efficient outcome?
s2-micro-03.stimulus: {"kind":"graph","description":"Market for leather sold by a tannery. Downward-sloping demand (marginal social benefit), upward-sloping private marginal cost (supply), and a higher marginal social cost curve parallel to it, lying $8 above it at every quantity. Market equilibrium at Q=10, P=$30; MSB meets MSC at Q=8.","data":{"x_axis":{"label":"Quantity of leather (hundreds of square feet)","min":0,"max":25,"unit":"hundreds of sq ft"},"y_axis":{"label":"Price / cost (dollars per hundred sq ft)","min":0,"max":50,"unit":"dollars"},"curves":[{"name":"Demand = Marginal social benefit (MSB)","equation":"P = 50 - 2Q","points":[[0,50],[25,0]]},{"name":"Supply = Private marginal cost (MC)","equation":"P = 10 + 2Q","points":[[0,10],[20,50]]},{"name":"Marginal social cost (MSC)","equation":"P = 18 + 2Q","points":[[0,18],[16,50]]}],"labeled_points":[{"label":"Market equilibrium","Q":10,"P":30},{"label":"Point where MSB = MSC","Q":8,"P":34}],"note":"The tannery's wastewater imposes a constant $8 cost per unit on downstream fishers, who are not party to the market."}

options.text: Too little leather is produced, because at 10 units the marginal social benefit of $30 is below the market price of $34.
options.why: Misconception: treating the efficient price of $34 as a market price and concluding underproduction; mixes up the direction of the externality's effect.

options.text: Too much leather is produced, because at 10 units the marginal social cost of $38 exceeds the marginal social benefit of $30.
options.why: Correct: at Q=10, MSB=30 and MSC=38, so the last unit costs society more than it benefits it; the efficient quantity is 8.

options.text: Too much leather is produced, because at 10 units the private marginal cost of $30 exceeds the marginal social benefit of $30.
options.why: Misconception: claims private MC exceeds MSB at 10, but they are equal at $30; ignores the external cost and reasons incorrectly from private equilibrium.

options.text: Too little leather is produced, because the efficient quantity of 8 units gives a higher price than the market price.
options.why: Misconception: assumes a higher price at the efficient point means the market produces too little; ignores that the efficient quantity (8) is smaller than the market quantity (10).

options.text: The market outcome is efficient, because quantity demanded equals quantity supplied at 10 units.
options.why: Misconception: equating market equilibrium with social efficiency; ignores the external cost not reflected in supply.

s2-micro-03.explanation_en: Efficiency requires producing where marginal social benefit equals marginal social cost. Solving 50 - 2Q = 18 + 2Q gives Q = 8, but the market, which counts only private cost, produces where 50 - 2Q = 10 + 2Q, so Q = 10. At 10 units the marginal social benefit is $30 while the marginal social cost is $38, so the last units cost society more than they are worth and too much leather is produced. The too-little options are wrong because the efficient quantity (8) is below the market quantity (10), and the $34 efficient price is not the market price. The private-marginal-cost option is wrong because private marginal cost equals marginal social benefit at 10 units; the gap comes from the $8 external cost. Equality of quantity demanded and supplied only shows the market clears, not that it is socially efficient.

s2-micro-04.stem: A market has inverse demand P = 100 − 2Q and a constant marginal cost of $20 per unit, which also equals average total cost. An economist compares the outcome predicted by the perfectly competitive model with the outcome predicted by the monopoly model for this same market. Which of the following statements correctly describes a difference between the two models' predictions?

stimulus.description: Abstract market with linear inverse demand and constant marginal cost, analyzed under two models.

data.marginal_cost: MC = 20 (constant, equal to average total cost)
data.model_1: Perfect competition: many price-taking firms, identical product, free entry
data.model_2: Monopoly: single seller, barriers to entry, firm faces the market demand curve
data.units: P in dollars per unit, Q in units

options.text: The monopoly model predicts a price of $20 and 20 units, while the competitive model predicts a price of $60 and 40 units.
options.why: Misconception: reverses the models, assigning the high price to competition and the low price to monopoly.

options.text: The monopoly model predicts a price of $60 and 40 units, while the competitive model predicts a price of $20 and 40 units.
options.why: Misconception: believes a monopolist produces the competitive quantity yet still charges a higher price, ignoring that MR lies below demand and a higher price requires a lower quantity along the demand curve.

options.text: The monopoly model predicts a price of $60 and 20 units, while the competitive model predicts a price of $20 and 40 units.
options.why: Correct: monopoly sets MR = 100 − 4Q = 20, so Q = 20 and P = 60 from the demand curve; competition sets P = MC = 20, so Q = 40.

options.text: The monopoly model predicts a price of $60 and 20 units, while the competitive model predicts a price of $20 and 20 units.
options.why: Misconception: applies the MR = MC rule to the competitive firm too, so it restricts output to 20 units and ignores that price-takers set P = MC.

options.text: The monopoly model predicts a price of $100 and 0 units, while the competitive model predicts a price of $20 and 40 units.
options.why: Misconception: confuses the demand intercept with the monopoly price, ignoring that the monopolist maximizes profit where MR = MC rather than charging the choke price.

s2-micro-04.explanation_en: Under monopoly, marginal revenue is MR = 100 − 4Q because the firm faces the downward-sloping market demand. Setting MR = MC gives 100 − 4Q = 20, so Q = 20, and the demand curve gives P = 100 − 40 = $60. Under perfect competition, firms are price takers and produce where P = MC, so 100 − 2Q = 20 and Q = 40 at a price of $20. The monopoly therefore charges a higher price and produces less. The option with a monopoly quantity of 40 units fails because a price of $60 corresponds to 20 units on the demand curve. The option reversing the models fails because monopoly has the higher price, not the lower. The option giving the competitive model 20 units fails because competitive firms equate price to marginal cost, not marginal revenue to marginal cost. The option with a $100 price and 0 units fails because that is the choke price, which would earn zero profit, whereas MR = MC yields a positive profit.

s2-micro-05.stem: An agricultural field station can use its fixed land, labor, and technology to produce wheat and sorghum. The table shows the maximum combinations it can produce. The station moves from point D to point E. Which of the following correctly states the opportunity cost of this move and explains why it differs from the opportunity cost of moving from point A to point B?

stimulus.description: Table of maximum combinations of wheat and sorghum a research farm can produce with all land and labor fully employed.

options.text: 1.2 thousand bushels of sorghum per thousand bushels of wheat, which is higher because the station's technology has deteriorated
options.why: Right number but wrong cause: the PPC is drawn with fixed technology, and a move along it does not change technology. Confuses movement along the PPC with an inward shift.

options.text: 1.2 thousand bushels of sorghum per thousand bushels of wheat, which is higher because resources are not equally productive in both crops
options.why: Correct: sorghum given up is 54-30=24 for 20 more wheat, so 1.2 per unit; A to B costs only 6/20=0.3, and the cost rises because resources are specialized, giving a bowed-out PPC.

options.text: 24 thousand bushels of wheat per thousand bushels of sorghum, which is higher because resources are not equally productive in both crops
options.why: Inverts the opportunity cost, mixing up which good is given up and misusing the magnitude 24 as a per-unit figure.

options.text: 0.3 thousand bushels of sorghum per thousand bushels of wheat, which is the same as moving from A to B because resources are equally productive in both crops
options.why: Uses the A-to-B cost of 0.3 and assumes constant opportunity cost, the straight-line PPC misconception.

options.text: 1.5 thousand bushels of sorghum per thousand bushels of wheat, which is higher because the station is producing inefficiently at point E
options.why: Uses the sorghum level at E (30) divided by 20 for 1.5 and wrongly claims E is inefficient, though every listed point is a maximum combination.

s2-micro-05.explanation_en: From D to E, wheat rises by 20 and sorghum falls from 54 to 30, a loss of 24, so the opportunity cost is 24/20 = 1.2 thousand bushels of sorghum per thousand bushels of wheat. From A to B it is only 6/20 = 0.3. The cost rises because resources are not equally productive in both crops; as more wheat is produced, land and labor better suited to sorghum must be shifted, giving a bowed-out PPC. The option blaming deteriorating technology is wrong because the table holds technology fixed and the move is along the curve. The option stating wheat given up per sorghum reverses the goods and the units. The option claiming 0.3 and equal productivity assumes constant opportunity cost, contradicted by the data. The option giving 1.5 miscalculates by using the sorghum level at E, and wrongly calls E inefficient, though all listed points are maximum combinations.

s2-micro-06.stem: Two food trucks, A and B, are the only sellers of lunch near an office park. Each truck simultaneously chooses a High or Low price, and the daily profits are shown in the payoff matrix. The game is played once and the trucks cannot make binding agreements. Which of the following correctly interprets the outcome?

stimulus.description: Payoff matrix for two food trucks, A and B, each choosing a High or Low lunch price. Payoffs are daily profit in dollars, listed as (Truck A, Truck B).

data.payoffs_units: dollars of daily profit, format (Truck A, Truck B)

options.text: Truck A chooses the Low price and Truck B chooses the High price, giving Truck A the largest possible profit of $400.
options.why: Misconception: believing one firm can exploit the other in equilibrium; Truck B would switch to Low (200 > 150) when A is Low, so this is not stable.

options.text: Both trucks choose the High price, because that outcome gives the largest combined daily profit of $600.
options.why: Misconception: assuming firms pick the joint-profit-maximizing outcome; ignores that High is not a best response to anything, so each truck has an incentive to cut price.

options.text: Both trucks choose the Low price, and their combined daily profit is $200 less than if both had chosen the High price.
options.why: Correct: Low is dominant for both trucks, so (Low, Low) is the Nash equilibrium with combined profit 400, which is 600 - 400 = $200 below the (High, High) combined profit.

options.text: Both trucks choose the Low price, and each truck earns $200 more per day than it would if both chose the High price.
options.why: Misconception: misreading the gap; at equilibrium each truck earns $100 less than at (High, High), not $200 more. It is the combined profit that is $200 lower.

options.text: Both trucks choose the High price, because each truck earns $300 and neither can gain by lowering its price.
options.why: Misconception: treating the cooperative outcome as an equilibrium; if the rival charges High, a truck earns 400 by choosing Low instead of 300, so each wants to deviate.

s2-micro-06.explanation_en: For Truck A, Low yields 400 versus 300 if B is High, and 200 versus 150 if B is Low, so Low is dominant. The same holds for Truck B by symmetry. The Nash equilibrium is therefore (Low, Low) with profits of $200 each, a combined $400. If both charged High, they would earn $300 each, or $600 combined, so the equilibrium combined profit is $200 lower: the prisoner's-dilemma result. The option with both trucks at High is wrong because each truck gains by undercutting, so it is not an equilibrium, even though it maximizes joint profit. The option with A Low and B High is wrong because B would switch to Low and earn 200 instead of 150. The option claiming each truck earns $200 more is wrong because each truck earns $100 less at equilibrium than at (High, High).

s2-micro-07.stem: The graph shows the domestic market for fitness trackers in a small country that can import any quantity at the world price. The government imposes a $20 per-unit tariff on imported trackers. Which of the following correctly explains the outcome of the tariff?

stimulus.description: Domestic market for fitness trackers: downward-sloping demand, upward-sloping supply, horizontal world price line at $50 and horizontal line at $70 showing the price with a $20 per-unit tariff.

data.assumptions: Small open economy; world supply is perfectly elastic at the world price.

options.text: Imports fall from 45,000 to 15,000, and foreign exporters pay the tariff, so domestic consumers are unaffected and surplus is unchanged.
options.why: Misconception: assumes the exporter bears the tariff; with a perfectly elastic world supply the domestic price rises by the full $20.

options.text: Imports fall from 45,000 to 15,000, and tariff revenue of $900,000 exceeds the consumer surplus lost, so total surplus rises.
options.why: Misconception: collecting the tariff on the original 45,000 imports instead of the remaining 15,000 (true revenue is $300,000), and ignoring deadweight loss.

options.text: Imports fall from 45,000 to 15,000, and domestic consumers buy more trackers because domestic producers sell more at the higher price.
options.why: Misconception: believes higher domestic production raises domestic consumption; quantity demanded actually falls from 75,000 to 65,000 as price rises.

options.text: Imports fall from 45,000 to zero, and domestic producers supply the entire quantity demanded at the $70 price.
options.why: Misconception: thinks any tariff eliminates imports; at $70 domestic supply is 50,000 and demand is 65,000, so 15,000 are still imported.

options.text: Imports fall from 45,000 to 15,000, and the consumer surplus lost exceeds the producer surplus gained plus tariff revenue, so total surplus falls.
options.why: Correct: CS loss 1,400 = PS gain 800 + revenue 300 + DWL 300, so total surplus falls by 300 (thousand dollars).

s2-micro-07.explanation_en: Free trade at $50: quantity demanded 75,000, supplied 30,000, imports 45,000. With the tariff the price is $70: demanded 65,000, supplied 50,000, imports 15,000. Consumer surplus falls by $1.4 million. Producers gain $0.8 million and the government collects 15,000 x $20 = $0.3 million. The remaining $0.3 million is deadweight loss, so total surplus falls. The option claiming $900,000 of revenue wrongly applies the tariff to the original imports and ignores deadweight loss. The option saying consumers buy more is wrong because quantity demanded falls as the price rises. The option saying imports drop to zero is wrong because 15,000 units are still imported. The option saying foreign exporters pay is wrong because the domestic price rises by the full tariff in a small open economy.

s2-micro-08.stem: An agricultural extension office runs the field trial shown in the table, varying only the number of workers on 10 fixed acres. Which of the following correctly describes the production relationship shown?

stimulus.description: Table of workers and total output of strawberries in a field trial on 10 fixed acres.

data.title: Field trial: 10 acres of land held constant; number of workers varied

options.text: Average product of labor stays constant because each added worker raises total output.
options.why: Misconception: confuses rising total output with constant average product; AP falls from 30 to about 21.7.

options.text: Marginal product of labor falls with every added worker, beginning with the first worker hired.
options.why: Misconception: assumes diminishing returns begin immediately; ignores that MP rises from 30 to 40 for the second worker.

options.text: Total output falls once more than five workers are hired because the sixth worker reduces output.
options.why: Misconception: confuses zero marginal product with negative marginal product; total output stays at 130, it does not fall.

options.text: Marginal product of labor rises for the first two workers and then diminishes, falling to zero for the sixth worker.
options.why: Correct: MP = 30, 40, 30, 20, 10, 0; it rises through worker 2, then diminishes to zero at worker 6.

options.text: Marginal product of labor is greatest for the sixth worker because total output is highest there.
options.why: Misconception: confuses total product with marginal product; MP of the sixth worker is the lowest (0).

s2-micro-08.explanation_en: Marginal product is the change in total output from one more worker: 30, 40, 30, 20, 10, 0. It rises for the second worker (specialization) and then diminishes, reaching zero for the sixth worker, so the first option is correct. Marginal product does not fall from the very first worker, because the second worker adds more (40) than the first (30). Total output does not fall at the sixth worker; it stays at 130, so marginal product is zero, not negative. Average product is not constant; it goes from 30 to 35 to 33.3 to 30 to 26 to 21.7. The sixth worker has the lowest marginal product, not the greatest, even though total output is highest at that point.

s2-micro-09.stem: A bakery has one oven that cannot be changed in the short run and hires additional workers as shown in the table. Which of the following correctly describes the production function shown?

stimulus.description: Table of the number of bakery workers and total loaves per day, with one oven fixed.

data.title: Daily production at a bakery with one oven (fixed input)

options.text: Diminishing marginal returns to labor begin with the second worker, because average output per worker is highest with one worker.
options.why: Confuses average product with marginal product; the second worker's MP (40) is actually higher than the first worker's (30).

options.text: Diminishing marginal returns to labor begin with the fifth worker, because total output first stops rising sharply at that point.
options.why: Confuses diminishing returns with output nearly leveling off; the fifth worker adds 10, but MP was already falling earlier.

options.text: Diminishing marginal returns to labor begin with the third worker, because the third worker adds fewer loaves than the second worker did.
options.why: Correct: MP of worker 2 is 40 and MP of worker 3 is 30, so marginal product first declines at the third worker.

options.text: Diminishing marginal returns to labor never occur, because total output never falls as more workers are hired.
options.why: Believes diminishing returns require total output to fall; they only require marginal product to fall while total output can still rise.

options.text: Diminishing marginal returns to labor begin with the sixth worker, because that worker adds no loaves to total output.
options.why: Thinks diminishing returns start only when marginal product reaches zero; MP began falling much earlier.

s2-micro-09.explanation_en: Marginal product is 30, 40, 30, 20, 10, 0 for workers 1 through 6. It rises for the second worker (40 > 30) and first falls with the third worker (30 < 40), so diminishing marginal returns begin with the third worker. The fifth-worker option is wrong because MP was already declining before output flattened. The second-worker option wrongly uses average product; the second worker's marginal product actually rises. The never-occur option wrongly requires total output to fall, but diminishing returns only require that marginal product decline. The sixth-worker option wrongly waits until marginal product is zero, when MP had been falling since the third worker.

s2-micro-10.stem: Using the estimates in the table, and assuming all other determinants of demand are unchanged, what is the expected change in the quantity of smartwatches demanded?

stimulus.description: Elasticity estimates for smartwatches and the expected changes in two market conditions.

data.title: Smartwatch demand estimates
rows: Cross-price elasticity of demand for smartwatches with respect to the price of basic fitness bands
Income elasticity of demand for smartwatches
Expected change in price of basic fitness bands
Expected change in price of smartwatches

options.text: An increase of 12%
options.why: Counts only the cross-price effect and ignores the income change.

options.text: An increase of 18%
options.why: Correct: cross-price effect 1.5 x 8% = +12% plus income effect 2.0 x 3% = +6%, total +18%.

options.text: An increase of 6%
options.why: Counts only the income effect and ignores the cross-price change.

options.text: An increase of 9%
options.why: Averages the two effects (12 and 6) instead of adding them.

options.text: A decrease of 6%
options.why: Sign error: treats the substitute's price rise as lowering demand (-12%) and then adds +6%.

s2-micro-10.explanation_en: Fitness bands and smartwatches are substitutes (positive cross-price elasticity), so an 8% rise in the band price raises smartwatch demand by 1.5 x 8 = 12%. Smartwatches are a normal good with income elasticity 2.0, so a 3% rise in income adds 2.0 x 3 = 6%. The smartwatch price is unchanged, so the total is +18%. The 12% answer omits the income effect. The 6% answer omits the cross-price effect. The 9% answer averages the effects rather than summing them. The decrease of 6% wrongly gives the cross-price effect a negative sign even though the goods are substitutes.

s2-micro-11.title: Cooperative Produce Market: Equilibrium, Surplus, and Elasticity

stimulus.description: Linear demand and supply for a farmers' cooperative selling tomatoes at a regional market, given as equations and a schedule.

data.setting: Field study at a regional farmers' market; good: crates of tomatoes per week
data.notes: Market is perfectly competitive with no taxes or price controls.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Using the demand and supply equations, find the equilibrium price and equilibrium quantity.
parts.model_answer: Set 100 - 5P = 10P - 20, so 15P = 120, P = $8 per crate and Q = 60 crates per week.

rubric_rows.criterion: Correct equilibrium price and quantity
alt_solutions: Reading P = 8, Q = 60 from the schedule where Qd = Qs
common_errors: Reporting only price or only quantity

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate consumer surplus and producer surplus at the equilibrium. Show your work.
parts.model_answer: Demand choke price is $20 (Qd = 0) and supply intercept is $2 (Qs = 0). CS = 0.5 x 60 x (20 - 8) = $360. PS = 0.5 x 60 x (8 - 2) = $180.

rubric_rows.criterion: Consumer surplus computed correctly
Producer surplus computed correctly
common_errors: Using 20 as the supply price intercept
Using base of 0 as the price floor, giving 240

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate the absolute value of the price elasticity of demand at the equilibrium price and quantity (point elasticity). Is demand elastic, inelastic, or unit elastic at this point? Justify your answer using your number.
parts.model_answer: |Ed| = |dQ/dP| x (P/Q) = 5 x (8/60) = 0.67 (2/3). Because 0.67 is less than 1, demand is inelastic at equilibrium.

rubric_rows.criterion: Correct elasticity value
Correct classification justified by comparison to 1
alt_solutions: Consistent classification with an incorrect c1 value, if justified by comparison to 1

stimulus.description: Payoff matrix for two fitness-app firms, Firm A (rows) and Firm B (columns), each choosing a High or Low monthly subscription price. Payoffs are annual profit in millions of dollars, listed as (Firm A, Firm B).

data.payoff_units: millions of dollars of annual profit

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify each firm's dominant strategy, if it has one, and state the Nash equilibrium of this one-time game. Use payoff numbers from the matrix to support your answer for Firm A.
parts.model_answer: Firm A: if B plays High, A earns 80 (Low) vs 60 (High); if B plays Low, A earns 45 (Low) vs 30 (High). Low is dominant for A, and by symmetry Low is dominant for B. Nash equilibrium: both choose Low price, payoffs (45, 45).

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies Low price as the dominant strategy, supported with Firm A payoff comparisons
required_elements: Low price dominant for both firms
Firm A compares 80 vs 60 and 45 vs 30
common_errors: Choosing High because the joint payoff is higher

rubric_rows.criterion: States the Nash equilibrium as (Low, Low) with payoffs 45 and 45

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the total profit of the two firms at the Nash equilibrium and the total profit if both firms charged the High price. By how much does the Nash equilibrium reduce combined profit?
parts.model_answer: Equilibrium: 45+45 = 90. Both High: 60+60 = 120. Reduction = 30 million dollars.

rubric_rows.criterion: Correctly computes 90, 120, and a difference of 30 million dollars

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Suppose the firms play this game every year for many years, and each firm threatens to charge the Low price forever if the other ever charges Low. Using numbers from the matrix, explain why Firm A might choose to keep the High price rather than cheat after Firm B charges High.
parts.model_answer: Cheating gains Firm A 80-60 = 20 million once. After that, B retaliates and A earns 45 instead of 60, losing 15 million every year. After two or more later years the losses (30 or more) exceed the 20 million gain, so A prefers to keep the High price.

rubric_rows.criterion: Computes the one-time gain from cheating (20 million) and the per-year loss after retaliation (15 million)
Concludes that repeated losses outweigh the one-time gain so A keeps High

s2-micro-13.title: Monopolist with Linear Demand and a Price Ceiling

stimulus.description: Abstract specification of a single-price monopolist: inverse demand P = 100 - 2Q, constant marginal cost and average total cost of 20. No figure is provided; students draw their own graph.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Draw a correctly labeled graph of the monopolist's market showing the demand curve, marginal revenue curve, marginal cost curve, and ATC curve. Label the profit-maximizing quantity Qm and price Pm, and label the vertical intercepts and the quantity-axis intercepts of demand and MR.
parts.model_answer: Axes: Quantity (horizontal, 0-50) and Price in dollars (vertical, 0-100). Demand is a downward-sloping line from (0,100) to (50,0). MR is a downward-sloping line from (0,100) to (25,0), twice as steep as demand. MC = ATC is a single horizontal line at $20. MR crosses MC at Qm = 20; go up to demand to find Pm = $60. Both Qm and Pm are labeled on the axes.

rubric_rows.criterion: Axes labeled (Price, Quantity) and a downward-sloping linear demand curve drawn and labeled with intercepts 100 (price) and 50 (quantity).
MR drawn below demand, from the same vertical intercept 100, with quantity intercept 25 (twice the slope of demand).
Horizontal MC = ATC line at $20 labeled.
Qm = 20 located where MR = MC, and Pm = 60 read from the demand curve above Qm, with both labeled.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the monopolist's economic profit. Then, on your graph, shade the area that represents the profit.
parts.model_answer: Profit = (60 - 20) x 20 = $800. Shaded rectangle: from Q = 0 to 20, between price 60 and ATC = 20.

rubric_rows.criterion: Profit of $800 calculated with work shown.
common_errors: Using total revenue of 1200 as profit

rubric_rows.criterion: Rectangle shaded between Pm=60 and ATC=20, from Q=0 to Qm=20.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate the deadweight loss of the monopoly relative to the perfectly competitive outcome, and shade the deadweight loss area on your graph.
parts.model_answer: Competitive quantity is where P = MC: 100 - 2Q = 20, so Q = 40. DWL = 0.5 x (60 - 20) x (40 - 20) = $400. The shaded triangle has vertices (20,60), (20,20), and (40,20).

rubric_rows.criterion: DWL = $400 calculated, with efficient quantity 40 identified.
Triangle shaded between demand and MC, from Qm=20 to Q=40.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Suppose the government imposes a binding price ceiling of $40 per unit. Calculate the quantity the monopolist now produces and its new profit, and explain, using marginal revenue, why the quantity rises compared with part (a).
parts.model_answer: With a $40 ceiling, the monopolist can sell any quantity up to 30 (where demand equals 40) at $40, so MR = $40 for Q up to 30. Since MR (40) exceeds MC (20) for every unit up to 30, it produces Q = 30. Profit = (40 - 20) x 30 = $600. The quantity rises because the ceiling makes MR equal to the ceiling price rather than falling below it, so MR stays above MC beyond Q = 20.

rubric_rows.criterion: Q = 30 and profit = $600 calculated.
Explains that the ceiling makes MR constant at $40 (above MC = 20) up to Q = 30, so producing more is profitable.
required_elements: MR equals ceiling price up to Q=30

s2-micro-14.stem: Researchers at a farmers' market recorded the weekly quantity of apples demanded at several prices before and after a nearby stand raised the price of pears, a substitute for apples. At a price of $4 per bag, quantity demanded rose from 50 to 65 bags. Which of the following best explains how this outcome occurs?

stimulus.description: Field experiment at a farmers' market: weekly bags of apples demanded at four prices, before and after a nearby stand raised the price of its pears (a substitute).

data.title: Weekly bags of apples demanded at a farmers' market
columns: Quantity demanded before pear price increase (bags)
Quantity demanded after pear price increase (bags)
data.note: Apple price per bag was set by researchers at each listed value; all other conditions unchanged. Pears are a substitute for apples.

options.text: The quantity demanded of apples increased along a fixed demand curve because the price of apples fell from $5 to $4.
options.why: Misconception: confuses a shift of demand with a movement along the curve; the apple price was held at $4 in both columns, so no own-price change occurred.

options.text: The demand for apples increased because the higher price of a substitute made apples relatively more attractive at every price.
options.why: Correct: a higher price of a substitute increases demand, shifting the whole curve right, so more is demanded at every price, including $4.

options.text: The demand for apples decreased because consumers expect the price of pears to keep rising, so they delay buying apples.
options.why: Misconception: gets the direction wrong; the data show 15 more bags at every price, an increase, and expecting higher pear prices would not cut apple demand.

options.text: The demand for apples increased because the higher price of pears lowered the price consumers pay for each bag of apples.
options.why: Misconception: right direction but wrong mechanism; the pear price change does not alter the price of apples, it shifts demand at an unchanged price.

options.text: The quantity demanded of apples increased because pears and apples are complements, so a pear price rise raises apple purchases.
options.why: Misconception: mislabels substitutes as complements and calls a change in quantity demanded; the cause is a demand shift, and complements would move opposite to the price of the other good.

s2-micro-14.explanation_en: At every price the quantity demanded of apples is 15 bags higher after the pear price rose, so the whole demand curve shifted right (an increase in demand). Because pears are a substitute, a higher pear price makes apples relatively more attractive, so buyers want more apples at each apple price. The option about a fall in the apple price from $5 to $4 is wrong: the apple price was fixed at $4 in both columns, and a price change would only move along one curve. The option about expected pear price rises causing a decrease in demand is wrong because the data show demand rose, not fell. The option claiming the pear price lowered what consumers pay for apples is wrong because the apple price did not change; demand shifted at the same price. The option calling the goods complements is wrong because pears and apples are substitutes, and a change in a related good's price shifts demand rather than changing quantity demanded.

s2-micro-15.stem: A farm stand runs a field experiment, changing the price of a pint of blueberries from $4.00 to $3.00 and recording daily sales as shown. Using the midpoint method, what is the price elasticity of demand over this price range, and what happens to the stand's total revenue when the price falls from $4.00 to $3.00?

stimulus.description: Field experiment at a farm stand: quantity of blueberry pints sold per day at two prices.

options.text: About 1.60 (elastic); total revenue increases
options.why: Uses the starting point as the base (40%/25%) instead of the midpoint, giving 1.60; the elasticity value is wrong even though the revenue direction is right.

options.text: About 0.86 (inelastic); total revenue decreases
options.why: Inverts the ratio (%ΔP/%ΔQ), getting 0.86 and concluding inelastic; revenue direction then follows that error, but revenue actually rises.

options.text: About 1.17 (elastic); total revenue increases
options.why: Correct: midpoint %ΔQ = 48/144 = 33.3%, %ΔP = 1/3.5 = 28.6%, ratio 1.17 > 1, so elastic; revenue rises from $480 to $504.

options.text: About 1.17 (elastic); total revenue decreases
options.why: Computes elasticity correctly but believes a price cut always lowers revenue, ignoring that elastic demand makes revenue rise when price falls.

options.text: About 0.86 (inelastic); total revenue increases
options.why: Inverts the ratio to 0.86 (inelastic) but pairs it with a revenue increase, which contradicts the total-revenue rule for inelastic demand.

s2-micro-15.explanation_en: Midpoint method: the change in quantity is 48 and the average quantity is 144, so %ΔQ is about 33.3%. The change in price is 1 and the average price is 3.50, so %ΔP is about 28.6%. Elasticity is 33.3/28.6, about 1.17, which is greater than 1, so demand is elastic. When demand is elastic, a price cut raises total revenue: revenue goes from 4 x 120 = $480 to 3 x 168 = $504. The 0.86 options invert the ratio. The 1.60 option uses the starting values as the base instead of the midpoints. The option pairing 1.17 with a revenue decrease contradicts the total-revenue rule, since elastic demand means price and revenue move in opposite directions. The option pairing 0.86 with a revenue increase is internally inconsistent and also rests on the inverted ratio.

s2-micro-16.title: Pollination Hives: Two Orchards in a Dilemma

stimulus.description: Payoff matrix for two neighboring orchards deciding whether to rent commercial pollination hives. Payoffs are annual profit in thousands of dollars, listed as (Orchard A, Orchard B).

data.units: thousands of dollars of annual profit

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Two neighboring orchards each choose, simultaneously and only once, whether to rent commercial pollination hives. Payoffs (annual profit, in thousands of dollars) are shown in the matrix. Does Orchard A have a dominant strategy? Identify it and justify your answer using payoff numbers from the matrix.
parts.model_answer: Yes. Renting hives is dominant for Orchard A: if B rents, A earns 40 by renting vs 20 by not renting; if B does not rent, A earns 70 by renting vs 60 by not renting. Renting pays more whatever B does.

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies Rent hives as Orchard A's dominant strategy
required_elements: Rent hives is dominant for A

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies with payoff comparisons for both of B's choices
required_elements: 70 vs 60 when B does not rent
common_errors: Compares A's payoff to B's payoff

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: State the Nash equilibrium of this game and the profit each orchard earns there. Then calculate how much more profit each orchard would earn if both did not rent instead.
parts.model_answer: Nash equilibrium: both rent hives, with profits of 40 each (thousand dollars). If neither rented, each would earn 60, which is 60 - 40 = 20 thousand dollars more per orchard.

rubric_rows.criterion: States equilibrium (Rent, Rent) with payoffs 40 and 40
Calculates 20 thousand dollars more per orchard

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Suppose a local rule fines an orchard 15 thousand dollars if it rents hives while the other orchard does not, so that orchard's payoff in that case falls by 15. Is (Do not rent, Do not rent) now a Nash equilibrium? Justify using Orchard A's payoffs.
parts.model_answer: Yes. With the fine, A's payoff from renting when B does not rent falls from 70 to 55, which is less than 60 from not renting. So A has no incentive to deviate, and by symmetry neither does B.

rubric_rows.criterion: Concludes yes and shows 55 < 60 (70 - 15 = 55) as the reason no orchard deviates
common_errors: Says the fine eliminates (Rent, Rent) as an equilibrium; it remains one

s2-micro-17.title: Two-Player Strategy Game: Interpreting Equilibrium Payoffs

stimulus.description: Payoff matrix for a simultaneous one-time game between Player X (rows A, B) and Player Y (columns C, D). Cells list (X payoff, Y payoff): A-C (6,6); A-D (2,8); B-C (8,2); B-D (3,3).

data.payoff_units: points (each payoff listed as X, Y)

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Does Player X have a dominant strategy? State yes or no and, if yes, identify it and use specific payoffs from the matrix to justify your answer.
parts.model_answer: Yes. Strategy B is dominant for X: if Y plays C, X gets 8 from B versus 6 from A; if Y plays D, X gets 3 from B versus 2 from A.

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies B as dominant and supports it with payoff comparisons for both Y choices
common_errors: Choosing A because (6,6) has the highest joint payoff

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Identify the Nash equilibrium of this game and state each player's payoff at that equilibrium.
parts.model_answer: Nash equilibrium is (B, D): X receives 3 and Y receives 3. By symmetry D is dominant for Y (8>6 against A; 3>2 against B).

rubric_rows.criterion: Names (B, D) with payoffs 3 for X and 3 for Y
required_elements: X plays B and Y plays D

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Compare the Nash equilibrium with the outcome (A, C). Calculate the total (X plus Y) payoff in each, and explain why the players do not reach (A, C) even though both would receive higher payoffs there.
parts.model_answer: Total at (B, D) = 3 + 3 = 6; total at (A, C) = 6 + 6 = 12. Each player has an incentive to deviate from (A, C): if Y plays C, X gains by switching to B (8 > 6), and likewise for Y. Because the game is played once without enforceable agreements, each pursues its dominant strategy and ends at (B, D).

rubric_rows.criterion: Gives both totals (6 and 12) and explains the incentive to deviate from (A, C), using a payoff
alt_solutions: Explains that (A,C) is not self-enforcing because each player's dominant strategy leads away from it

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Suppose the payoff in cell (B, C) changes from (8, 2) to (5, 2); all other payoffs stay the same. Does the Nash equilibrium change? State yes or no and justify using Player X's best responses.
parts.model_answer: No. If Y plays D (still dominant for Y), X compares 3 from B with 2 from A, so B is still X's best response. (B, D) remains the equilibrium at (3,3). X's best response to C changes to A (6 > 5), but Y never plays C.

rubric_rows.criterion: States the equilibrium does not change and justifies with X's best response to D (3 > 2) and/or Y's dominant D
alt_solutions: Notes that Y's strategy D is unaffected so X still best responds with B
common_errors: Claiming (A,C) becomes the equilibrium because A now beats B against C

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Suppose instead the two players repeat this game many times and each threatens to play its dominant strategy forever if the other ever does. Using payoffs from the matrix, explain why cooperation at (A, C) may now be sustained.
parts.model_answer: A one-time deviation from (A, C) earns 8 instead of 6 (a gain of 2), but triggers punishment that leaves the deviator with 3 per round instead of 6 (a loss of 3 each later round). If future payoffs matter enough, the long-run loss outweighs the one-time gain, so cooperation can be sustained.

rubric_rows.criterion: Compares the short-run deviation gain (8 vs 6) with the long-run punishment loss (3 vs 6) using numbers
required_elements: repeated interaction makes future losses outweigh the gain
common_errors: Saying the matrix payoffs themselves change
